location: Picasso, Miro, Dali: Unbound exhibition at MFA, Boston, MA

rows.stop: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)
rows.text: The result was an illustrated book featuring 40 color lithographs, bound in luxurious publisher’s vellum, challenging the boundaries of visual and verbal storytelling. Gifted to the Museum of Fine Arts by Boris Fridman, this piece enhances the museum's collection, further emphasizing the importance of collaborative artistry in bookmaking. Displayed in the Linde Family gallery, this work is nestled within a broader context of masterpieces that continue to redefine the relationship between text and image. Fridman's donation not only enriched the museum's holdings but also allowed the public to witness how a book can serve as a canvas for extraordinary artistic expression.
rows.orientation: The Picasso, Miro, Dali: Unbound exhibition at MFA in Boston delves into the world of the livre d'artiste (artist's book), showcasing how these revolutionary works by Spanish artists transformed the book into a unique art form. Within Gallery 184, you will encounter three extraordinary pieces: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers), Au Soleil du Plafond, and Moses and Monotheism. These works, deeply collaborative ventures, offer a glimpse into the intersection of images, words, and typography, bridging the tangible world with realms of imagination and faith. Discover how Freud's unconventional theory about Moses challenges traditional beliefs at Moses and Monotheism, and witness Fridman's book-turned-canvas donation at Le Lézard aux plumes d’or. Your first stop is Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers). Stand directly in front of "Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)" by Joan Miró to fully appreciate the symphony of color and form within this illustrated book. From this perspective, you can immerse yourself in the intricate interplay between image and text, a hallmark of the livre d'artiste tradition.

rows.text: Gris created 11 lithographs on Arches paper, chosen for its capacity to enhance the printed image and preserve the vibrant intricacies of his Cubist designs. This medium enabled Reverdy's poetic narratives to resonate alongside Gris's abstract visuals. This collaboration between Gris and Reverdy exemplifies a revolutionary approach to art-making, where the synergy of illustration and poetry produces a unified work of art. In that spirit, the exhibition at MFA Boston offers a rare glimpse into such innovative encounters, usually kept hidden in archives. As you stand beneath "Au Soleil du Plafond," consider how Gris and Reverdy transformed a simple book into an immersive artistic experience.
rows.orientation: Stand beneath the elegant ceiling installation of "Au Soleil du Plafond" and look upwards. From this vantage point, the delicate interplay of light and shadow brings forth the textures of the lithographs, revealing the harmonious blend of image and text that Gris and Reverdy sought to achieve.

rows.text:
In 1974, Salvador Dalí took on the challenge of illustrating Sigmund Freud’s seminal text "Moses and Monotheism," merging surrealist art with psychoanalytic theory. Dalí's choice to create a set of ten illustrations—using drypoints and lithographs on sheepskin—brought an organic texture to Freud’s exploration of faith's historical roots, creating a unique set that stands apart in the exhibition. Freud, known for developing psychoanalysis, authored the original work in 1939, proposing that Moses was an Egyptian noble and not a Hebrew slave, which challenged conventional beliefs. By engaging with these groundbreaking ideas, Dalí’s work beckons viewers to reconsider the invisible forces of faith and identity that continue to shape our reality.

That's 3 stops — Freud's 1939 work posited Moses as Egyptian, not Hebrew, challenging beliefs and Gris and Reverdy turned a book into immersive art at "Au Soleil du Plafond.".
